questions.explanation: Incidence requires following a population forward from a defined starting point without the outcome to observe new cases. Case-control studies start with people who already have the outcome and look backward, making forward-time measurement impossible. Option A is incorrect (case-control studies have controls). Options B and D mischaracterize the design. Option E is a bias, not the structural reason.

questions.question_text: A researcher suspects that sleep deprivation increases the risk of depressive episode onset. To test this hypothesis by prospectively following sleep-deprived and non-sleep-deprived adolescents over 3 years and measuring subsequent depression diagnosis, which study design is most appropriate?

options.text: Case-control study of past sleep patterns
Cross-sectional survey of sleep and mood
Cohort study identifying exposed (sleep-deprived) and non-exposed groups and following forward
Randomized controlled trial of sleep deprivation
Ecological study of school districts

correct_answer.text: Cohort study identifying exposed (sleep-deprived) and non-exposed groups and following forward

questions.explanation: This design requires assembling groups based on exposure (sleep deprivation status), then following forward prospectively to measure outcome (depression onset). This defines cohort study design and allows measurement of incidence and relative risk. Option A is retrospective. Option B is snapshot. Option D would be unethical. Option E is population-level. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a major disadvantage of case-control studies?

options.text: They are too time-consuming and expensive
They are unsuitable for studying multiple etiological factors
They are highly prone to selection and recall bias
They require active intervention in exposed subjects
They cannot be used in hospital-based populations

correct_answer.text: They are highly prone to selection and recall bias

questions.explanation: The source explicitly identifies selection and recall bias as major disadvantages of case-control studies. These retrospective biases occur because data collection depends on memory and past records. Option A is wrong—case-control studies are noted for being less time-consuming and less expensive. Option B contradicts the advantage of studying multiple etiological factors. Option D describes experimental designs. Option E is factually incorrect. ---

questions.question_text: A case-control study of first-episode psychosis recruits cases from four urban psychiatric hospitals and controls from general medical patients at the same hospitals, all matched on age and sex. The study finds a strong association between childhood neurological abnormalities (measured via medical records review) and psychosis. What is the primary strength of using hospital records for exposure measurement in this study?

options.text: It eliminates recall bias that would occur with subjective reporting
It ensures all study subjects have been thoroughly medically evaluated
It prevents selection bias by using objective data sources
It allows measurement of relative risk instead of odds ratio
It guarantees the temporal sequence of exposure preceding outcome

correct_answer.text: It eliminates recall bias that would occur with subjective reporting

questions.explanation: Childhood neurological abnormalities documented in medical records represent objective, contemporaneous data recorded without memory bias. This avoids the substantial recall bias vulnerability of case-control studies when relying on subject memory of past events. Using documented records from the time the abnormalities occurred provides more reliable exposure data than retrospective patient recall. However, this does not ensure all subjects are thoroughly evaluated (selection bias remains possible with differential medical record documentation). Hospital records do not change the measure of association from odds ratio. Temporal sequence is established by exposure occurring in childhood before psychosis onset, regardless of data source.

questions.question_text: In a case-control study, what is the maximum control-to-case ratio that increases statistical power?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states Up to a ratio of 4:1, when the number of controls is increased, the power of a study increases. But not after exceeding this ratio. This means 4:1 is the optimal ratio beyond which additional controls do not meaningfully increase power.

questions.question_text: A cross-sectional prevalence study measures both social isolation and depressive symptoms in a community sample. The study finds that individuals who are more socially isolated have higher depression severity. Which type of analytical limitation does this study encounter?

options.text: Cannot determine if social isolation causes depression, depression causes isolation, or a third factor causes both
Cannot include enough subjects to detect associations
Cannot identify any association between the variables
Can only be conducted in hospital settings
Cannot measure outcomes with adequate precision

correct_answer.text: Cannot determine if social isolation causes depression, depression causes isolation, or a third factor causes both

questions.explanation: The simultaneous measurement of exposure and outcome in a cross-sectional design means any three causal scenarios are possible but indistinguishable from the data: isolation causing depression, depression causing isolation, or a third variable (e.g., anxiety disorder) causing both. This bi-directionality problem is inherent to cross-sectional designs. Cross-sectional studies can detect associations and can be community-based. Statistical power and measurement precision are separate issues.

questions.question_text: [CASE VIGNETTE] A clinician-researcher in a community mental health center enrolls 300 patients currently taking antipsychotics and follows them for 3 years, monitoring for metabolic side effects. No control group receives a different treatment; all subjects continue their current medications. This is best described as:

options.text: Randomized controlled trial
Uncontrolled experimental study
Case series with prospective follow-up
Ecological study of clinic populations
Case-control study

correct_answer.text: Case series with prospective follow-up

questions.explanation: This is a prospective descriptive study of multiple subjects (case series) with follow-up over time, monitoring outcomes in a single group without experimental manipulation or comparison group. Option A requires randomization and comparison. Option B would involve experimental intervention manipulation. Option D uses population-level analysis. Option E is retrospective with comparison groups. ---

questions.question_text: A census differs from a typical cross-sectional study in that a census:

options.text: Includes the whole population instead of a subset sample
Measures outcomes prospectively over time
Involves random intervention assignment
Focuses on rare diseases exclusively
Requires longitudinal follow-up

correct_answer.text: Includes the whole population instead of a subset sample

questions.explanation: Census as a special cross-sectional study where the sample includes the whole population rather than a subset. Options B and C describe features of different study designs. Options D and E are not characteristics of census design. ---

questions.question_text: A case-control study is best described as which type of research design?

options.text: Experimental with prospective data collection
Retrospective analytical study starting from defined outcome groups
Cross-sectional study measuring exposure and outcome simultaneously
Descriptive study with no comparison groups
Prospective cohort design with random intervention assignment

correct_answer.text: Retrospective analytical study starting from defined outcome groups

questions.explanation: Case-control studies are explicitly retrospective designs that begin by identifying cases (diseased) and controls (non-diseased), then look backward to collect exposure data. Option A is incorrect because case-control studies are observational, not experimental. Option C confuses case-control with cross-sectional design. Option D ignores the comparative (analytical) nature of case-control studies. Option E describes experimental/prospective design, not case-control. ---

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to compare the long-term prognosis of early-onset versus late-onset bipolar disorder in terms of functional recovery, relapse rates, and mortality over 20 years. Which study design best answers this prognostic question?

options.text: Case-control study comparing prognosis between early and late-onset cases
Cohort study following both groups prospectively over time
Cross-sectional comparison of both groups at a single time point
Ecological study of population bipolar disorder trends
Experimental RCT with random assignment to early or late-onset groups

correct_answer.text: Cohort study following both groups prospectively over time

questions.explanation: The source explicitly identifies cohort studies as the best design for answering prognostic questions. Following both early-onset and late-onset cohorts forward over 20 years allows direct measurement of outcomes (recovery, relapse, mortality) in each group. Case-control studies start from outcome (prognosis already determined), making them inappropriate for prognostic questions. Cross-sectional studies provide snapshot data, not longitudinal prognosis. Ecological studies are population-level. Random assignment to age of onset is impossible.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to understand the lived experience and meaning of depression in adolescents. Which study design and methodology would be most appropriate?

options.text: Case-control study with standardized questionnaires
Randomized controlled trial with outcome measurement
Qualitative study
Ecological study of hospital admission rates
Cross-sectional prevalence survey

correct_answer.text: Qualitative study

questions.explanation: That qualitative studies are appropriate for exploring the 'meaning' and 'health experience' of conditions. Options A is analytical. Option B is experimental. Option D is population-level. Option E is descriptive but not focused on meaning/experience. ---

questions.question_text: Which of the following represents the fundamental difference between a cohort study and a case-control study in terms of temporal direction?

options.text: Cohort studies are descriptive; case-control studies are analytical
Cohort studies follow people forward from exposure to outcome; case-control studies start from outcome and look back to exposure
Cohort studies measure prevalence; case-control studies measure incidence
Cohort studies use matched controls; case-control studies do not
Cohort studies are experimental; case-control studies are observational

correct_answer.text: Cohort studies follow people forward from exposure to outcome; case-control studies start from outcome and look back to exposure

questions.explanation: Cohort studies as observational studies of people followed over a period of time to detect events/outcome (prospective), while case-control studies are retrospective, starting with outcomes and examining prior exposure. Option A confuses design taxonomy. Option C reverses the measures. Option D is incorrect about matching. Option E is partly wrong (both are observational unless randomized).

questions.question_text: A cross-sectional study is best described as measuring what?

options.text: Incidence of disease over a prolonged period
Exposure and outcome at a single point in time
Temporal relationship between exposure and disease
Effect of a deliberately assigned intervention
Probability of disease given exposure

correct_answer.text: Exposure and outcome at a single point in time

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies are explicitly described as measuring exposure and outcome together at a single point in time—referred to as a snapshot and also called prevalence studies. Option A describes longitudinal/cohort studies. Option C requires prospective follow-up. Option D describes experimental studies. Option E refers to relative risk calculation in cohort designs.

questions.question_text: How would overmatching on a putative causal factor affect a case-control study?

options.text: Increase the statistical power of the study
Eliminate selection bias entirely
Reduce the observed risk difference between groups
Increase the ability to detect the association
Improve recruitment of controls

correct_answer.text: Reduce the observed risk difference between groups

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states overmatching can also reduce the risk difference between the two groups and may inadvertently result in matching for putative causal factors. By controlling for a true risk factor through matching, the observable difference between cases and controls diminishes, weakening the apparent association. Options A, B, D, and E misrepresent the consequences of overmatching.
